summary: Marswalk is a browser-based EVA planner and 3D walkable simulation built on real NASA data from Gale Crater, Mars. Mission planners choose science stops, and an A* route planner finds the safest path for walking or driving. It works on 80,000 terrain cells from the USGS 1 m HiRISE elevation model and weighs slope, roughness, daylight, suit consumables and radiation dose. Users then walk or drive the planned route in a 3D world built from the real terrain. They survey sites with Curiosity's own Navcam images, map hydrated minerals with MRO CRISM data, face REMS-based temperatures and dust storms, and send reports to Earth that wait for the real light-time delay. We tested the planner against reality. Along 9.8 km of Curiosity's actual drives, the rover stayed off our no-go terrain 15 times more often than chance. A scenario tool ranks every stop order, vehicle and start time in milliseconds. This matters because the first crewed Mars EVAs will be planned without real-time help from Earth. Marswalk shows how open NASA data can support trustworthy, explainable traverse planning. It also makes that planning tangible and engaging for anyone with a web browser.
details:
What it does and how it works

Marswalk is a Mars EVA (spacewalk) planner and a walkable 3D simulation built on real NASA data from Gale Crater, where the Curiosity rover is exploring lower Mount Sharp. It runs entirely in a web browser: https://shivenlak.github.io/MarsWalker/

  • Plan: on a mission map the crew picks science stops (the Gediz Vallis channel, the boxwork ridges, Curiosity's drill sites and the rover itself). An A* path planner searches 80,000 terrain cells from the USGS 1 m HiRISE elevation model, weighing slope, roughness, walking speed on each grade and the crew's maximum safe slope (adjustable live). The plan reports time, distance, climb, suit oxygen and power, radiation dose and sunset margin, and flags any stop that can't be reached safely.
  • Compare: a what-if tool plans every combination of stop order, on foot or by buggy, and start time in milliseconds, then ranks them.
  • Validate: we checked the planner's hazard map against 9.8 km of Curiosity's real drives. The rover stayed off our no-go terrain 15 times more often than chance. We also report honestly that A* does not copy Curiosity's exact routes, because the rover often detoured for science.
  • Walk it: the plan becomes a 3D world built from the real terrain: HiRISE colour on the 1 m terrain with Mount Sharp on the horizon from HRSC-MOLA data; Curiosity's real wheel tracks, stopping points and Navcam photos; MRO CRISM mineral maps that place the specimens; REMS-based temperatures, dust storms that dim sunlight realistically and cold nights; an autopilot that follows the A* route even at x60 time warp; a second astronaut (EV2) who fetches samples on their own A* route; a pressurised buggy and a habitat; and reports to Earth that wait for the real speed-of-light delay (about 11 minutes each way today).

Benefits and intended impact

The first crewed Mars EVAs will be planned without real-time help from Earth. Marswalk shows that open NASA data can support traverse planning that is explainable and checked against reality; every number is either sourced or clearly labelled as an assumption. It also makes mission planning tangible for students and the public: anyone with a browser, phone or VR headset can stand on real Martian ground and see why a route was chosen.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: TypeScript and Python.
  • Web app: Three.js (3D, WebXR for VR), Leaflet (maps), Vite. No backend; hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Data pipeline: Python with rasterio, NumPy and Pillow, pulling only our area of interest from multi-gigabyte NASA/USGS files into compact web formats (about 10 MB first load).
  • Testing: 26 automated tests (Vitest), including the Curiosity validation and the Earth-Mars distance check against NASA's published figures.
  • Development: built with AI coding assistance (Claude Code).

Creativity

Marswalk combines a serious planning tool with a game you can actually play. You plan with real science and then live with the results: night falls, oxygen runs low, a dust storm cuts visibility and you have to trust the route home. A 30-second self-running demo, photo mode, touch controls and VR support make it easy for anyone to try.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: sources logged, assumptions labelled, weak points reported alongside strengths.
  • Crew safety: slope and roughness limits, point of no return, suit consumables and radiation dose.
  • Real mission constraints: daylight, communication delay, dust season and the buddy system for EVAs.
  • Accessibility: runs in a browser, works on phones and VR headsets, loads quickly.
  • Scope: one real, science-rich area instead of the whole planet.
